title: What Made This Sand?
sub: Grades 1–2 · Under the Microscope · Moon dust and Earth’s sand

hero.credit: Siim Sepp, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

objective: Children will look closely at sand, first with a magnifying glass and then in photographs taken down real microscopes. They will learn that Earth’s sand is shaped by **wind, water and living things**, and that Moon dust was made in a different way: by space rocks hitting the Moon over billions of years. That is why its grains are sharp and jagged, and why they stick to everything.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Up close, every grain has a story. Looking carefully is how scientists find out where something came from.

items.text: describe sand grains up close: their shape, color and size
items.question: describe sand grains up close?

items.text: name three things that shape Earth’s sand: wind, water and living things
items.question: name what shapes Earth’s sand?

items.text: say how Moon dust was made, and why its grains are sharp
items.question: say how Moon dust was made?

items.text: match a sand to what shaped it, and give a clue you can see
items.question: match a sand to what shaped it, and give a clue?

materials: A cup of sand from a playground, a beach or a garden shop; magnifying glasses, one between two if you can
A pinch of flour and a dark cloth or piece of felt
Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed; *Under the Microscope* on a screen if you have one
Differentiated handouts, one per child; crayons
questions: What shapes can you see? Are the grains round, smooth, sharp or flat?
Are all the grains the same color?
Which sand was shaped by water? How can you tell?
Why is Moon dust sharp, when desert sand is rounded?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *Under the Microscope*, children wipe a slide, place a sample, focus, magnify and explore, then compare Moon dust with Earth’s soil side by side. The display case holds a real lunar meteorite and sand specimens from around the world.
**On the poster** *Our Incredible Moon*, find the paragraph about Moon dust at the bottom.

steps.title: A mystery picture
script: Show the picture on the screen or page 3 without saying what it is. *“What do you think this is?”* Take guesses: pebbles, beads, sweets. Then pass round the cup of sand and the magnifying glasses. *“It’s sand! Sand from the Gobi Desert, in Mongolia, seen down a microscope. The whole picture is only 10 millimeters wide: about as wide as a fingernail.”*

img.credit: Siim Sepp, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

screen.caption: What do you think this is?

steps.purpose: Wonder at something ordinary made strange, before anyone says what it is.
students: What do you think this is?
What colors and shapes can you see?

steps.title: Shaped on Earth
script: Show the three Earth sands. Read the poster’s words: Earth’s soil *is shaped by wind, water, and living things.* The Gobi Desert sand was shaped by the **wind**: look how rounded its grains are. The Vistula River sand was shaped by **water**: its grains are smooth and glassy. The Bermuda sand was shaped by **living things**: it is full of pieces of coral and shells, and tiny pink grains that give Bermuda’s beaches their pink color.

steps.title: Made by space rocks
script: Now show the Moon soil. China’s *Chang’e 6* mission brought it back in 2024, from the far side of the Moon. The Moon has no wind, no rivers and no living things to shape it. Read: *“Unlike Earth’s soil, which is shaped by wind, water, and living things, lunar dust is formed over billions of years through meteorite impacts.”* Meteorites are space rocks. Over billions of years, space rocks crashing into the Moon made its dust.

steps.purpose: Meet real Moon soil, and hear how it was made.
students: What do you notice about these grains?
How is it different from Earth’s sand?

steps.title: Moon and Earth
script: Put the two side by side. Read: *“This makes the dust particles sharp and jagged, and they can stick to everything because of static electricity.”* Astronauts said Moon dust smelled like gunpowder and was hard to clean off their suits.

steps.title: Does it stick?
script: Rub a pinch of flour onto the dark cloth, then a pinch of sand. Shake the cloth. The sand falls off; the flour clings. Flour is not Moon dust, but it is very fine, like Moon dust. In the exhibition’s *Under the Microscope* room, wiping Moon dust off a slide works the same way: it clings to the cloth, while Earth’s grains brush aside. If you have a screen, let a child try it.

steps.purpose: Feel the poster’s difference: fine dust clings, sand brushes off.
students: Rub a pinch of flour on the cloth. Then a pinch of sand.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Then children choose a handout. All three levels match the same Earth sands to what shaped them, and compare them with Moon dust.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Draw a line from each sand to what shaped it: wind, water or living things. Circle the words for Moon dust, then draw what you saw through the magnifying glass.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Write the letter of each sand beside what shaped it. Finish three sentences from a word bank, then draw Moon dust and Earth’s sand side by side.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Match each sand and write the clue that gave it away. Write how Moon dust is different from Earth’s sand, then wonder about a mystery slide: round glass beads from the Moon.

steps.purpose: Match the sands on paper, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same sands and the same Moon dust.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back as questions, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, children show a thumb up, sideways or down. For the last, ask a Red Level child to name a clue.
